point: 用“吗”的是非问句 · Yes/no questions with 吗
title: 1. 用“吗”的是非问句 Yes-no questions with “ma 吗”
explanation: When the interrogative modal particle “吗” is added to the end of a declarative sentence, it becomes a “yes-no” question. The answer is the affirmative or negative form of the declarative sentence without “吗”. For example,

patterns.label: Declarative sentence → Interrogative sentence
examples: 我叫马大为。 → 你叫马大为吗？

point: 形容词谓语句 · Adjectival predicate
title: 2. 形容词谓语句 Sentences with an adjectival predicate
explanation: In Chinese, an adjective can function directly as a predicate and can be modified by adverbs such as “hěn 很” (very) and/or “yě 也” (also), etc., for example: “Wǒ hěn hǎo. 我很好。” (I'm fine.), “Dàwéi yě hěn hǎo. 大为也很好。” (Dawei is fine too.) The negative form is made by placing the adverb “bù 不” (not) before the adjective, as in “Wǒ bù máng. 我不忙。” (I'm not busy.)

examples.es: I'm fine.
Dawei is fine too.
I'm not busy.

notes: Notes: ❶ The adverbs “很”, “也”, “不”, etc. must be placed before the adjective they modify.

❷ If a sentence has no other adverb (for example, “不”, “也”, “tài 太”, etc.), the adverb “很” is usually added. For example, to answer “Nǐ zuìjìn zěnmeyàng? 你最近怎么样？” (How have you been lately?), the answer is not “* Wǒ hǎo. 我好。” or “* Wǒ máng. 我忙。”, but “Wǒ hěn hǎo. 我很好。” (I'm very well.) or “Wǒ hěn máng. 我很忙。” (I'm very busy.) In this context, “很” does not necessarily carry the literal meaning of “very”.

❸ When a sentence with an adjectival predicate is turned into a question ending in “吗”, “很” is usually dropped. For example, “我很好。” (I'm very well.) → “Nǐ hǎo ma? 你好吗？” (How are you?). One does not ask “* Nǐ hěn hǎo ma? 你很好吗？”.

point: 副词“也”的位置 · Position of 也
title: 3. 副词“也”的位置 The position of the adverb “yě 也” (also)
explanation: The adverb “也” must be placed after the subject but before the verb or adjective functioning as the predicate. For example, “Wǒ yě hěn hǎo. 我也很好。” (I'm fine too.), but one does not say “*Yě wǒ hěn hǎo. 也我很好。” or “*Wǒ hěn hǎo yě. 我很好也。” In addition, “也” cannot function as a predicate on its own; for example, it is not correct to say “* wǒ yě 我也”.
In a negative sentence, “也” must be placed before “不”.

patterns.label: Negative
patterns.formula: 也 + 不 + Verb/Adjective (Subject + 也不 + Verb/Adjective)

examples.es: I'm fine too.

notes: Incorrect: *也我很好。 / *我很好也。 / *我也。

title: 4. 汉语的语序 Word order in Chinese
explanation: Chinese grammar has several main characteristics. Strictly speaking, it has no inflection for personal pronouns, verb tense, gender, singular or plural, etc. Grammatically, word order plays an extremely important role. In Chinese, the subject, that is, the topic being described, usually comes first, and the predicate, which describes the subject, comes after it. For example,

title: ② Qǐng jìn. Please come in.
explanation: “qǐng 请 + verb” is a polite way of making a request.

examples.es: Please come in.

notes: Related note (PDF p. 47): ② Qǐngwèn…… May I ask... (Excuse me, ...) This is a polite way of addressing someone to ask a question.

title: ③ Nǐ zuìjìn zěnmeyàng? How have you been?
explanation: “…… zěnmeyàng 怎么样？” (How is/are...?) is often used to ask about the situation of someone or something. “Nǐ (zuìjìn) zěnmeyàng? 你（最近）怎么样？” is a greeting used between acquaintances or friends. The answer can be “hěn hǎo 很好” (very well), “hěn máng 很忙” (very busy), etc.

examples.es: How have you been?
very well
very busy

notes: ④ Nǐ ne? And you? (How are you?)

point: Tones of 一 and 不
title: 1. Tone change of “yī 一” (one) / (3) Tone change of “bù 不” (not)
explanation: The original tone of “yī 一” (one) is the first tone. When it appears alone or at the end of a word or sentence, it is read in its original tone. When it is used as an ordinal number (i.e. dì-yī 第一 first), it is also read in its original tone. However, when “一” comes before a first, second or third tone, it is read in the fourth tone. When it comes before a fourth tone, it is read in the second tone.
The original tone of “bù 不” is the fourth tone, but when it is used before a fourth tone, it is read in the second tone “bú 不”.

patterns.label: 一 before 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone
patterns.formula: yī + ˉ / ˊ / ˇ → yì + ˉ / ˊ / ˇ

examples.es: a glass of
a bottle of
a volume, a copy
once
first

notes: (4) Brief summary of the tone change rules (PDF p. 16): ① Third-tone change: When two third-tone syllables are read aloud together, the first third tone changes to the second tone (ˇ + ˇ → ˊ + ˇ). When a third-tone syllable comes before a first, second, fourth or most neutral tones, it is read aloud as a half-third tone. ② Tone change of “yī 一” (one): yī + ˉ/ˊ/ˇ → yì + ˉ/ˊ/ˇ; yī + ˋ → yí + ˋ.
一 is introduced in Lesson 1 (Introduction to phonetics) and 不 in Lesson 2 (Introduction to phonetics, PDF p. 30).

title: 1. “是”字句（1） Sentences with “shì 是” (to be) (1)
explanation: In a sentence with “是”, the verb “是” is used to link two related parts, which can be nouns, pronouns or noun phrases. The negative form is made by adding “bù 不” (not; read in the second tone, bú) before “是”. Unless it is specially emphasized, “是” is usually pronounced lightly.

patterns.label: Negative
patterns.formula: Subject + 不 + 是 + Noun/Noun phrase

patterns.label: Question
patterns.formula: Subject + (Adverb) + 是 + Noun/Noun phrase + 吗？

notes: Note: The negative adverb “不” must be placed before “是”.

point: 用疑问代词的问句(1)：什么、哪 · Question words 什么 / 哪
title: 2. 用疑问代词的问句（1）：什么、哪 Questions with interrogative pronouns (1): “shénme 什么” (what) or “nǎ 哪” (which)
explanation: In Chinese, the word order of a question with an interrogative pronoun is the same as the word order of a declarative sentence.

patterns.label: Declarative sentence → Interrogative sentence
patterns.formula: The interrogative pronoun (什么 / 哪) takes the place of the word being asked about; the word order does not change
examples: 这是饺子。 → 这是什么？
北京人喜欢吃面条儿和饺子。 → 北京人喜欢吃什么？
他是美国人。 → 他是哪国人？

examples.zh: 北京人喜欢吃面条儿和饺子。
examples.pinyin: Běijīngrén xǐhuan chī miàntiáor hé jiǎozi.

point: 连词“和” · The conjunction 和
title: 3. 连词“和” The conjunction “hé 和” (and)
explanation: The conjunction “和” usually connects pronouns, nouns or noun phrases, as in “tā hé tā 她和他” (she and he), “bàba hé māma 爸爸和妈妈” (dad and mom), and “wǒ māma hé nǐ māma 我妈妈和你妈妈” (my mom and your mom). The conjunction “和” cannot connect two clauses and is rarely used to connect two verbs or two adjectives.

examples.es: she and he
dad and mom
my mom and your mom

examples.pinyin: Bāozi hé jiǎozi dōu hěn hǎochī.

point: 副词“都”的位置 · Position of 都
title: 4. 副词“都”的位置 The position of the adverb “dōu 都” (all; both)
explanation: Like “yě 也” (also), the adverb “都” must be placed after the subject but before the verb or adjective of the predicate. For example, “Bāozi hé jiǎozi dōu hěn hǎochī. 包子和饺子都很好吃。” (Both the baozi and the jiaozi are delicious.) You cannot say “* Dōu bāozi hé jiǎozi hěn hǎochī. 都包子和饺子很好吃。” because it is grammatically incorrect. When “都” and “也” appear in the same sentence, “也” precedes “都”, for example, “Wǒ bàba hé wǒ māma yě dōu hěn máng. 我爸爸和我妈妈也都很忙。” (My dad and mom are also both very busy.)

patterns.label: Subject | Predicate (Adverb + Verb/Adjective)
examples: 丁力波和马大为都很好。
你爸爸和你妈妈都是北京人吗？
王小云和宋华也都不喜欢吃面条儿。

examples.pinyin: Bāozi hé jiǎozi dōu hěn hǎochī.
examples.es: Both the baozi and the jiaozi are delicious.

examples.zh: 我爸爸和我妈妈也都很忙。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ bàba hé wǒ māma yě dōu hěn máng.
examples.es: My dad and mom are also both very busy.

examples.zh: 丁力波和马大为都很好。
examples.pinyin: Dīng Lìbō hé Mǎ Dàwéi dōu hěn hǎo.
Wǒ hé Lín Nà dōu bú tài máng.

examples.zh: 你爸爸和你妈妈都是北京人吗？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bàba hé nǐ māma dōu shì Běijīngrén ma?

examples.zh: 王小云和宋华也都不喜欢吃面条儿。
examples.pinyin: Wáng Xiǎoyún hé Sòng Huá yě dōu bù xǐhuan chī miàntiáor.

notes: Incorrect: *都包子和饺子很好吃。

title: ⑤ Nín guìxìng? Wǒ xìng Chén. May I ask your surname? My surname is Chen.
explanation: This is a polite way of asking someone's surname. Note that when answering, you cannot use “* Wǒ guìxìng 我贵姓……”; you must say “Wǒ xìng 我姓……” (you can add “Wǒ jiào 我叫……”). The word “guì 贵” can only be used together with “nǐ 你” (you) or “nín 您” (you, polite), but cannot be used with “wǒ 我” (I) or “tā 他 / 她” (he/she).

examples.es: May I ask your surname?
My surname is Chen.

notes: ④ Nín hǎo! Hello! The respectful form of “nǐ 你” is “nín 您”. This polite expression is often used to address elderly people or someone of an older generation. It can also be used among people of the same generation out of courtesy. People in Beijing are very fond of using this form of address.
Incorrect: *我贵姓……

title: ⑦ Wǒ shì Měiguórén. I'm American.
explanation: The word “rén 人” after the name of a country indicates someone's nationality, for example:
Měiguó 美国 (United States) —— Měiguórén 美国人 (American)
The word “人” after a place name indicates someone's ancestral home or birthplace, for example,
Běijīng 北京 (Beijing) —— Běijīngrén 北京人 (person from Beijing)

examples.es: I'm American.
American
person from Beijing

notes: ⑥ Nǐ shì nǎ guó rén? What country are you from?

title: 1. “有”字句 Sentences with “yǒu 有” (to have)
explanation: A sentence with the verb “有” in the predicate usually expresses possession. The negative is formed by putting “méi 没” before “有”. Note: “bù 不” is not used before “有”.

If the subject of a sentence with “有” is an organization, a place or a location, the verb “有” also means “there is/there are”, for example: “Nǐmen jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén? 你们家有几口人？” (How many people are there in your family?)

patterns.label: Question
examples: 他女儿今天有英语课吗？

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen jiā yǒu sì kǒu rén.

examples.zh: 他女儿今天有英语课吗？
examples.pinyin: Tā nǚ'ér jīntiān yǒu Yīngyǔkè ma?
Nǐmen jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
examples.es: How many people are there in your family?

notes: Note: “bù 不” is not used before “有”.

point: 表领属关系的定语 · Possessive modifier with 的
title: 2. 表领属关系的定语 Attributives expressing possession
explanation: In Chinese, a modifier, also known as an attributive, is always placed before the word it modifies. When a pronoun or a noun is used as a modifier to express possession, the structural particle “de 的” is usually required.

When a personal pronoun modifies a noun referring to a family member, workplace or residence, “的” can be omitted. For example, “wǒ māma 我妈妈” (my mom), “nǐ nǚ'ér 你女儿” (your daughter), “tāmen jiā 他们家” (their home/family).

patterns.label: Omission of 的 (family member, workplace or residence)

examples.es: my mom
your daughter
their home/family

notes: Related note (Notes L3, PDF p. 93, ① Nǐmen jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?): When a personal pronoun modifies a place, an organization or a workplace, spoken Chinese often uses the plural form of the pronoun. For example, “nǐmen jiā 你们家” (your home), “wǒmen xuéxiào 我们学校” (our school), and “wǒmen guójiā 我们国家” (our country).

point: 数量词做定语 · Number + measure word
title: 3. 数量词做定语 “Numeral + measure word” as a noun modifier
explanation: In modern Chinese, a number generally cannot modify a noun on its own; to do so it must be combined with a measure word. Usually each noun has its own measure word.

The measure word “个” is commonly used before nouns referring to people, things, workplaces, etc. It is read in the neutral tone. The measure word “张” is generally used for objects with a flat surface such as paper, pictures and business cards. The measure word “口” is used to express the number of people in a family. For example, “wǔ kǒu rén 五口人” (five members in the family). In other cases, “个” must be used. For example, “Wǒmen bān yǒu shí gè rén. 我们班有十个人。” (There are 10 people in our class.) One cannot say: “*Wǒmen bān yǒu shí kǒu rén. 我们班有十口人。”

examples.es: five members in the family

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bān yǒu shí gè rén.
examples.es: There are 10 people in our class.

notes: Note: When the demonstrative pronoun “zhè 这” (this) or “nà 那” (that) is used as a modifier, there must also be a measure word before the modified noun. For example, 这张照片, 那个朋友.
Incorrect: *我们班有十口人。

point: 用疑问代词的问句(2)：谁、几 · Question words 谁 / 几
title: 4. 用疑问代词的问句（2）：谁、几 Questions with interrogative pronouns (2): “shéi 谁” (who) or “jǐ 几” (how many)
explanation: In a question with the pronoun “谁” or “几”, the word order is the same as in a declarative sentence. You only need to use the question word “谁” or “几” to replace what you don't know and want to ask about. The word “谁” is used to ask about people, while “几” is used to ask about a number smaller than 10.

patterns.label: Declarative sentence → Interrogative sentence
patterns.formula: 谁 / 几 replaces the part being asked about; the word order does not change
examples: 那是我哥哥。 → 那是谁？
王小云喜欢吃点心。 → 谁喜欢吃点心？
这是林娜的照片。 → 这是谁的照片？
我们家有四口人。 → 你们家有几口人？
她今年五岁。 → 她今年几岁？

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì Lín Nà de zhàopiàn.
Wǒmen jiā yǒu sì kǒu rén.
Nǐmen jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?

notes: Related note (Notes L3, PDF p. 96, ② Nǐ nǚ'ér jīnnián jǐ suì? How old is your daughter this year?): The expression “Jīnnián jǐ suì? 今年几岁？” (How old... this year?) is often used to ask a child's age. Note: It is not used to ask an adult's age.

point: 还(1)：表示补充 · 还 = also, in addition
title: 5. 还（1）：表示补充、追加 The adverb “hái 还” (1): Indicating “in addition”
explanation: One of the uses of “还” is to make an additional remark. For example, “Wǒ yǒu liǎng gè jiějie, hái yǒu yí gè gēge. 我有两个姐姐，还有一个哥哥。” (I have two older sisters and also an older brother.)

patterns.label: Additional remark
examples: 我有两个姐姐，还有一个哥哥。
我有一个哥哥，还有两个弟弟。

examples.zh: 我有两个姐姐，还有一个哥哥。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu liǎng gè jiějie, hái yǒu yí gè gēge.
examples.es: I have two older sisters and also an older brother.

examples.zh: 我有一个哥哥，还有两个弟弟。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí gè gēge, hái yǒu liǎng gè dìdi.
Wǒ yào kāfēi, hái yào diǎnxin.

notes: The last two examples come from Exercise I of this section.

title: ① Nǐmen jiā zhēn piàoliang! Your home is really beautiful!
explanation: The word “zhēn 真” (truly, really), placed before an adjective, often expresses an exclamation.

examples.es: Your home is really beautiful!

notes: The second example is key sentence no. 6 of the lesson (PDF p. 97).

point: 称数法 · 几 and 多少
title: 1. 11～100 的称数法 Numbers from 11 to 100
explanation: When you ask a question about a number greater than or equal to “shí 十” (ten), you must use the interrogative pronoun “duōshao 多少”. The measure word after “多少” is often omitted. For example,

examples.zh: A: 你们班有多少（个）学生？
examples.es: How many students are there in your class?

examples.zh: B: 我们班有三十个学生。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bān yǒu sānshí gè xuésheng.
examples.es: There are 30 students in our class.

notes: Note ② 你们班一共有多少人？ (How many people are there in your class in total?): The two interrogative pronouns “jǐ 几” (how many) and “duōshao 多少” (how many/how much) are used to ask about numbers. “几” is often used to ask about a number smaller than 10. A measure word must be placed between “几” and the noun, as in “jǐ kǒu rén 几口人” (how many family members). “多少” can be used to ask about any number; it may or may not be accompanied by a measure word. For example, to ask “how many photos?”, you can say “duōshao zhāng zhàopiàn 多少张照片” or “duōshao zhàopiàn 多少照片”.

point: 钟点读法 · Telling the time
title: 2. 钟点读法 Telling the time
explanation: These words are used to tell the time in Chinese: “diǎn (zhōng) 点钟” (o'clock), “kè 刻” (quarter), and “fēn 分” (minute). For example, “bā diǎn èrshíwǔ fēn 八点二十五分” (eight twenty-five). In Chinese, the time is told in the following ways:

patterns.label: Telling the time
patterns.formula: number + 点 (+ number + 分 / 刻 / 半)
examples: 2:00 两点（钟）（“钟” is often omitted.）
2:05 两点零（líng, zero）五分（When “分” is used with a number smaller than 10, “零” must be added before the number.）
2:12 两点十二（分）（When “分” is used with a number greater than 10, “分” can be omitted.）
2:15 两点一刻 o 两点十五（分）
2:30 两点半 o 两点三十（分）
2:45 两点四十五（分）o 差一刻三点
2:55 两点五十五（分）o 差五分三点

notes: Note ② 下午两点一刻还有口语课。(I also have spoken Chinese class at 2:15 in the afternoon.): When the number “2” is combined with a measure word, “liǎng 两” is used instead of “èr 二”. For example, “liǎng gè jiějie 两个姐姐” (two older sisters), “liǎng zhāng zhàopiàn 两张照片” (two photos), “liǎng diǎn yí kè 两点一刻” (a quarter past two). You cannot say “*二个姐姐”, “*二张照片” or “*二点一刻”. When the number “2” is used on its own, for example in “yī 一, èr 二, sān 三……” (one, two, three...), or appears in a larger number, “二” is still used even if a measure word follows the “2”, as in “shí'èr 十二” (twelve), “èrshí'èr 二十二” (twenty-two), “èrshíliù gè nǚshēng 二十六个女生” (twenty-six female students), “shí'èr gè nánshēng 十二个男生” (twelve male students), “shí'èr diǎn 十二点” (twelve o'clock), etc.

point: 表时间的词语做状语 · Time expressions
title: 3. 表时间的词语做状语 Time expressions used as adverbials
explanation: Time expressions such as “xiànzài 现在” (now), “jīntiān 今天” (today), “xiàwǔ 下午” (afternoon) can function as adverbials to indicate the time of an action or state. A time adverbial can be placed before or immediately after the subject. In other words:
(1) after the subject and before the verb or adjective (see the first table below), or
(2) before the subject to emphasize the time (see the second table below).

patterns.label: Table 1
patterns.formula: Subject + Time adverbial + Verb plus object/Adjective
examples: 林娜今天下午三点半练习口语。

patterns.label: Table 2
patterns.formula: Time adverbial + Subject + Verb plus object/Adjective
examples: 下午四点我还有口语课。

examples.zh: 林娜今天下午三点半练习口语。
下午四点我还有口语课。

notes: Notes ❶ A time adverbial can never be placed after the predicate. For example, one cannot say “* Wǒ yǒu kè jīntiān. 我有课今天。”

Notes ❷ If there is more than one time word in an adverbial, the larger unit of time must come before the smaller one. For example, “jīntiān xiàwǔ 今天下午” (this afternoon) and “míngtiān shàngwǔ bā diǎn bàn 明天上午八点半” (tomorrow at 8:30 in the morning).

point: 正反疑问句 · Affirmative-negative questions (V不V)
title: 4. 正反疑问句 Affirmative-negative questions: verb/adjective-not-verb/adjective (A-not-A questions)
explanation: The affirmative and negative forms of a sentence's predicate can also be juxtaposed to form a question. In other words, a verb or an adjective plus “not” plus the same verb or adjective can also form a question.
An answer to this type of question can be a complete sentence (affirmative or negative) or a sentence with its subject or object omitted. For example, the answers to the questions above are:
To answer a “shì bu shì 是不是” question like the one shown in the last example of the table above, one can say “是” (affirmative answer) or “不是” (negative answer). For example,

patterns.label: Question
patterns.formula: Verb/Adjective + 不 / 没 + Verb/Adjective + Object

examples.zh: （他妈妈）是（老师）。/ 是，他妈妈是老师。
（他妈妈）不是（老师）。/ 不是，他妈妈不是老师。

point: 用“呢”构成的省略问句 · Questions with 呢
title: 6. 用“呢”构成的省略问句 Elliptical questions ending in “ne 呢”
explanation: Putting “呢” after a pronoun or a noun (phrase) turns it into an elliptical question. The content must already have been clearly expressed before you can ask the question ending in “呢”.

patterns.label: Elliptical question
examples: 我很好。你呢？（你呢？= 你好吗？）
王小云学英语专业。马大为呢？（马大为呢？= 马大为学什么专业？）
我们班有二十六个女生。你们班呢？（你们班呢？= 你们班有多少个女生？）

examples.zh: 王小云学英语专业。马大为呢？
我们班有二十六个女生。你们班呢？

title: ④ 我们一起去吧。 Let's go together.
explanation: The modal particle “ba 吧” is often used at the end of a statement to soften the tone. It is used to make a suggestion or a request, give advice or an order, or start a discussion.

examples.es: Let's go together.

notes: Vocabulary (p. 4): 吧 ba Pt.m. — modal particle used at the end of a sentence to indicate consultation, suggestion, request, etc. 一起去吧 坐吧

title: ⑤ 恐怕不行。 I'm afraid not.
explanation: “Kǒngpà bùxíng. 恐怕不行。” is an expression used to politely turn down a suggestion.

examples.es: I'm afraid not.

notes: Vocabulary (p. 4): 恐怕 kǒngpà Adv. — (indicating an estimate) I'm afraid...; 行 xíng V — to be OK 不行

title: ③ 对了，你明天晚上有没有时间？ By the way, do you have time tomorrow evening?
explanation: “duìle 对了” (by the way; oh, right) is often used in colloquial conversation to express a spontaneous idea or thought, to change the subject of a conversation, or to remind the listener of a new topic.

examples.zh: 对了，你明天晚上有没有时间？
examples.es: By the way, do you have time tomorrow evening?

notes: Vocabulary (p. 4): 对了 duìle V — (expression used to change the subject of a conversation or to remind the listener of a new topic) by the way; oh, right

title: 吧 · Guessing: “…, right?”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Suggestions with "ba"” and “Softening speech with "ba"” — not from the textbook
explanation: Put 吧 (ba) at the end of a statement and say it with a question tone, and you get a question that already contains your guess: “…, right?” / “I suppose…?”. You think you know the answer and you only want the other person to confirm it.
Compare it with 吗: 你是林娜吗？ is an open yes/no question (you have no idea). 你是林娜吧？ means “You're Lin Na, aren't you?” — you're fairly sure, maybe because someone described her to you.

It is the same particle as the 吧 of suggestions you saw in L4 (我们走吧), which the Wiki explains first. The difference is the content: a suggestion proposes an action (often with 我们 or a command), while a guess states a fact you want confirmed. The Wiki points out that something like 我们六点去吧？ is “more of a confirmation than a suggestion”.
吧 also softens a statement in general (应该是吧 “it should be, I think”), which is why a guess with 吧 sounds polite and not too direct.

examples.es: You're Lin Na, right?
He's your older brother, isn't he?
I suppose you're Americans?
You must be tired today, right?

examples.pinyin: ——Nǐ shì lǎoshī ba? ——Bú shì, wǒ shì xuésheng.
examples.es: “You're a teacher, I guess?” “No, I'm a student.”
Wrong: 吗 and 吧 never go together — choose one.
Wrong: 吧 doesn't go with question words like 谁 or 什么; the guess must be a full statement.

notes: Answer a 吧 question like a 吗 question: 是/对 to confirm, 不是 to correct.
The Wiki has no separate article for this “guessing” 吧; it treats it alongside suggestions and softening (“Suggestions with "ba"”, “Softening speech with "ba"”).
Your course material doesn't explain this point: the L4 Notes only explain 吧 for suggestions, requests and advice.

title: 1. 年、月、日和星期的读法 Expressing dates and the days of the week
explanation: In Chinese, the four numbers that make up the name of a year are read as four separate digits, with “nián年” at the end. For example, “一九九八年” is read as “yī jiǔ jiǔ bā nián” (1998).
The numbers that make up the name of a month are read with “yuè月” at the end. For example,
Dates are formed by combining a number from 1 to 31 with “hào号” in the spoken form or “rì日” in the written form. For example,
If it is a date in the current month, one can omit “月” and simply say “号”. For example, “Zhège Xīngqīrì jǐ hào? 这个星期日几号？” (What is the date this Sunday?)

The names of the days of the week begin with the word “xīngqī星期”, followed by a number from one to six, indicating Monday to Saturday. In China, the week begins on Monday and ends on Sunday, which is called “Xīngqīrì 星期日” or “Xīngqītiān 星期天”. Saturday and Sunday are days off and are called “zhōumò周末” (weekend).
The order of the date and time is expressed as follows:

patterns.label: Years
examples: 一九八八年 yī jiǔ bā bā nián (1988)
二〇〇〇年 èr líng líng líng nián (2000)
二〇〇二年 èr líng líng èr nián (2002)
二〇二〇年 èr líng èr líng nián (2020)

patterns.label: Days of the month
examples: （十一月）二十二日 (Shíyīyuè) èrshí'èr rì November 22
（十二月）三十一日 (Shí'èryuè) sānshíyī rì December 31

patterns.label: Days of the week
patterns.formula: 星期 + 一…六 / 日 / 天

patterns.label: Order of date and time
patterns.formula: 年 + 月 + 日 + 星期 + 上午 / 下午 / 晚上 + 钟点 (year + month + day + day of the week + morning / afternoon / evening + time)
examples: 二〇二〇年十二月二十五日星期五晚上八点二十五 (8:25 in the evening, Friday, December 25, 2020)

examples.es: What is the date this Sunday?

examples.zh: 二〇二〇年十二月二十五日星期五晚上八点二十五
examples.es: 8:25 in the evening, Friday, December 25, 2020

title: 2. 名词谓语句 Sentences with a nominal predicate
explanation: Nouns, noun phrases and number-measure word compounds can act as the predicate of a sentence without the verb “shì 是”. This type of sentence is used especially in spoken language to express age, time, etc. It is also used to express price or birthplace.
The negative form of a sentence with a nominal predicate uses “bú shì 不是”.

patterns.label: Affirmative / Question
examples: 这个星期日十月二十五号。

patterns.label: Negative
patterns.formula: Subject + 不是 + Number and measure word

examples.es: Today is not the 5th (of the month).
She is not 32 years old.

point: 双宾语动词谓语句(1)：送、教 · Double objects
title: 3. 双宾语动词谓语句（1）：送、教 Sentences with a double-object verbal predicate (1): “sòng 送” (to give as a gift) or “jiāo 教” (to teach)
explanation: Verbs such as “送”, “教”, among others, can take two objects. The first object refers to people and the second refers to things.

patterns.label: Subject + Verb + Object₁ + Object₂
patterns.formula: 送 / 教 + Pronoun/Noun (Person) + Noun/Noun phrase (Thing)
examples: 林娜送她哥哥一个大蛋糕。

examples.zh: 林娜送她哥哥一个大蛋糕。

notes: Notes ❶ A verb or a verb phrase can act as the object of a verb, as in “Lǎoshī jiāo wǒ xiě. 老师教我写。” (The teacher taught me to write.), “Xiǎoyún jiāo wǒ zuò shòumiàn. 小云教我做寿面。” (Xiaoyun taught me to make longevity noodles.), and “Tā xǐhuan chī miàntiáor. 她喜欢吃面条儿。” (She likes eating noodles.)
Notes ❷ In Chinese, only some verbs can take two objects.

title: 4. “就”（1）：表示强调 The adverb “jiù 就” (1): Expressing emphasis
explanation: The adverb “就” placed before a verb emphasizes what follows it. For example, “Tā jiù shì wǒ gēge. 他就是我哥哥。” (He is my older brother.), “Zhè jiù shì shòumiàn. 这就是寿面。” (These are longevity noodles.)

examples.es: He is my older brother.
These are longevity noodles.

title: 5. 疑问语调句 Questions with rising intonation
explanation: A statement with a rising intonation, without a final “ma 吗”, can also form a question. In writing, a question mark must be added at the end of the sentence. This type of question often expresses uncertainty or disbelief.

examples.es: You know my younger sister?
You're coming to our class?
You're studying English?

point: Notes L5 · 多大 / 几岁
title: ② 你哥哥今年多大？ How old is your older brother?
explanation: Here “duō 多” is an adverb which, followed by an adjective, is used to ask a question. “dà 大” in this case refers to one's age. To ask an adult's age in Chinese, one should use “多大” (how old) or “duō dà suìshu 多大岁数” (what age). The question “jǐ suì 几岁” can only be used to ask a child's age.

examples.es: How old is your older brother?

point: Notes L5 · 咱们 / 我们
title: ⑤ 咱们 we
explanation: When the speaker uses “zánmen 咱们”, the listener is included; “wǒmen 我们” may or may not include the listener.
notes: Vocabulary (p. 33): 咱们 zánmen Pron. — we; 干杯 gānbēi VO — to make a toast; cheers 咱们干杯

title: ③ 我来介绍一下。 Let me introduce (you).
explanation: When “yíxià 一下” is used after a verb, it often indicates a brief action or an attempt. It also serves to soften the tone of the expression so that it sounds less formal. For example, “rènshi yíxià 认识一下” (get acquainted) and “nǐ kàn yíxià 你看一下” (take a look).

examples.es: Let me introduce (you).
get acquainted
take a look

title: ② 祝你生日快乐！ Happy birthday!
explanation: This is a common way of wishing others a happy birthday. “Zhù nǐ 祝你……” (I wish you…) is an expression used for holidays or simply to send someone your best wishes before an event. For example, “Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè! 祝你新年快乐！” (Happy New Year!) and “Zhù nǐ gōngzuò shùnlì! 祝你工作顺利！” (I wish you success at work!) On the other hand, the expression “zhùhè 祝贺” is used to congratulate someone on something that has already happened. For example, if a person has graduated or gotten married, etc., the expression “zhùhè nǐ 祝贺你” (congratulations) is often used.

examples.es: Happy birthday!
Happy New Year!
I wish you success at work!
congratulations

title: 1. 方位词 Locative nouns (nouns of locality)
explanation: Words such as “lǐbian 里边” (inside), “wàibian 外边” (outside), “zuǒbian 左边” (left), “yòubian 右边” (right), “pángbiān 旁边” (beside), “shàngbian 上边” (above), “xiàbian 下边” (below), “qiánbian 前边” (in front), “hòubian 后边” (back; behind), “dōngbian 东边” (east), “xībian 西边” (west), “nánbian 南边” (south), “běibian 北边” (north), and “duìmiàn 对面” (opposite) are locative nouns. They can be used as subject, object or modifier. They can also be modified.

examples.pinyin: Qiánbian yǒu méiyǒu yí gè fànguǎn?
examples.es: Is there a restaurant across the street?
The bank is to the east of the library.

examples.zh: 右边的楼是新同学的宿舍楼。
examples.pinyin: Yòubian de lóu shì xīn tóngxué de sùshèlóu.
examples.es: The building on the right is the new students' dormitory.

notes: Notes ❶ When a locative noun is used as a modifier, “de 的” must be used between the modifier and the word modified. For example, “yòubian de lóu 右边的楼” (the building on the right) and “qiánbian de chāoshì 前边的超市” (the supermarket in front). When the locative noun is the word being modified, there is usually no “的” before it. For example, “xuéxiào lǐbian 学校里边” (inside the school) and “shítáng pángbiān 食堂旁边” (next to the cafeteria).

Notes ❷ The word “lǐbian 里边” is generally not used after the name of a country or a very large place. For example, one can say “zài Zhōngguó 在中国” (in China) and “zài Běijīng 在北京” (in Beijing), but not “* 在中国里边” or “* 在北京里边”.

Notes ❸ Usually monosyllabic words such as “lǐ 里” (in; inside), “wài 外” (out; outside), “qián 前” (front), “hòu 后” (back), “shàng 上” (up), “xià 下” (down), “dōng 东” (east), “xī 西” (west), etc. are not used alone, but are often modified by other nouns, for example: “xuéxiào li 学校里” (in the school), “xiàomén wài 校门外” (outside the school gate), “lóu shàng 楼上” (upstairs), “lóu xià 楼下” (downstairs), “lù dōng 路东” (east side of the road), among others. These monosyllabic words can also modify other nouns, for example, “qián mén 前门” (front door), “hòu mén 后门” (back door), “nán lóu 南楼” (south building), and “běi lóu 北楼” (north building).

point: 用“在”表方位 · Location with 在
title: 2. 用“在”表方位的句子 Sentences with “zài 在” (to be at/in) indicating location
explanation: To express the idea that someone or something is located in a certain place, “在” is usually used as the main verb of the sentence. The subject of this type of sentence is usually a person or thing. The object is the noun indicating the location.

patterns.label: Affirmative / Question / Negative
patterns.formula: Subject (Person or Thing) + (不) 在 + Object (Locative noun)
examples: 大为的宿舍在学校里边吗？

examples.zh: 大为的宿舍在学校里边吗？

point: 用“有”“是”表存在 · Existence with 有 / 是
title: 3. 用“有”“是”表存在的句子 Sentences with “yǒu 有” (there is) or “shì 是” (to be) indicating existence
explanation: To indicate the existence of someone or something in a certain place, “有” or “是” is often used as the main verb of the predicate. The subject (topic) of this type of sentence is usually a locative noun or noun phrase. The object is usually a noun or noun phrase indicating the person or thing.

patterns.label: With 有 (affirmative / negative / question)
patterns.formula: Subject or Topic (Locative noun or noun phrase) + 有 / 没有 / 有没有 + Object (Person or Thing)
examples: 前边有没有一个小饭馆？

patterns.label: With 是 (affirmative / negative / question)
patterns.formula: Subject or Topic (Locative noun or noun phrase) + 是 / 不是 / 是不是 + Object (Person or Thing)
examples: 图书馆东边不是教学楼。
你对面是不是一个银行？

examples.zh: 图书馆前边有一个宿舍楼。
examples.pinyin: Túshūguǎn qiánbian yǒu yí gè sùshèlóu.
examples.es: There is a dormitory building in front of the library.

examples.zh: 图书馆前边是我们的宿舍楼。
examples.pinyin: Túshūguǎn qiánbian shì wǒmen de sùshèlóu.
examples.es: In front of the library is our dormitory building.

examples.zh: 我们的宿舍楼在图书馆前边。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen de sùshèlóu zài túshūguǎn qiánbian.
examples.es: Our dormitory building is in front of the library.

notes: Note: A sentence with “是” and a sentence with “有” differ in the following ways: The object of a sentence with “有” refers to places, people or things in general, while the object of a sentence with “是” refers to a specific place, person or thing. Therefore, we can say “Túshūguǎn qiánbian yǒu yí gè sùshèlóu. 图书馆前边有一个宿舍楼。” (There is a dormitory building in front of the library.), but we do not say “*Túshūguǎn qiánbian yǒu wǒmen de sùshèlóu. 图书馆前边有我们的宿舍楼。” To express this, we can say “Túshūguǎn qiánbian shì wǒmen de sùshèlóu. 图书馆前边是我们的宿舍楼。” (In front of the library is our dormitory building.) or “Wǒmen de sùshèlóu zài túshūguǎn qiánbian. 我们的宿舍楼在图书馆前边。” (Our dormitory building is in front of the library.)

point: 介词结构(1)：跟 / 给 · 跟 and 给
title: 4. 介词结构（1）：跟 / 给 + 代词 / 名词 Prepositional constructions (1): “gēn 跟” (with) / “gěi 给” (to; for) + Pronoun/Noun
explanation: The preposition “跟” is often combined with a noun or a pronoun to form a prepositional phrase. It is placed before the verb, indicating the manner in which an action is performed.
The preposition “给”, when combined with a noun or a noun phrase, forms a prepositional phrase. When placed before the verb, the prepositional phrase indicates the recipient of the action.

patterns.label: 给
examples: 马大为给大家唱英语歌。

examples.es: Come with me.
Let me introduce you.

examples.zh: 马大为给大家唱英语歌。

notes: Note: The prepositional phrase with “跟……” or “给……” must be placed before the verb. You can only say “Nǐ gēn wǒ lái. 你跟我来。” (Come with me.) or “Wǒ gěi nǐ jièshào yíxià. 我给你介绍一下。” (Let me introduce you.)

title: 5. 用“……，好吗？”“……，对吗？”提问 Questions with “……, hǎo ma 好吗?” or “……, duì ma 对吗?”
explanation: The question “……, hǎo ma 好吗？” is often used to make a suggestion and ask for other people's opinion. The first half of the sentence is a suggestion. The affirmative answer can be “hǎo a 好啊” or “hǎo 好”, etc. The negative answer is normally not “*bù hǎo 不好”, but “zhēn bù hǎoyìsi 真不好意思，……”, “duìbuqǐ 对不起……”, “kǒngpà bùxíng 恐怕不行”, etc.

The question “……, duì ma 对吗？” is often used to indicate that the speaker is asking with a certain degree of certainty and confidence. The first part of the sentence can be affirmative or negative. The answer could be “duì对” or “bú shì 不是”.

patterns.label: Suggestion
examples: 我们买一个大蛋糕，好吗？

examples.zh: 我们买一个大蛋糕，好吗？
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen mǎi yí gè dà dàngāo, hǎo ma?
examples.es: How about we buy a big cake? (Literally, let's buy a big cake, OK?)

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jiāo wǒ Hànyǔ, hǎo ma?
examples.es: Could you teach me Chinese? (Literally, teach me Chinese, OK?)
You're Chinese, right?

examples.zh: B: 对，我是中国人。/ 不是，我是西班牙人。
examples.pinyin: Duì, wǒ shì Zhōngguórén. / Bú shì, wǒ shì Xībānyárén.
examples.es: Yes, I'm Chinese. / No, (I'm not Chinese,) I'm Spanish.

title: ① 别着急，林小姐。 Don't worry, Miss Lin.
explanation: The adverb “bié 别” placed before a verb or an adjective (别 + verb/adjective) expresses dissuasion or prohibition. Here, Song Hua jokingly calls Lin Na “Miss Lin” to help her relax.

examples.es: Don't worry, Miss Lin.

notes: Vocabulary (p. 56): 别 bié Adv. — don't 别客气 别看 别去

point: 百、千的称数法 · Numbers up to 9999
title: 百、千的称数法 · Numbers from 100 to 9,999
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Structure of numbers” and “Comparing "er" and "liang"” — explanation not from the textbook (number table from Básico 2, PDF p. 81)
explanation: Big numbers are read the way they are written: each digit followed by its unit — 千 (thousands), 百 (hundreds), 十 (tens), then the last digit. 2543 = 两千 五百 四十 三.

Zeros: if there's a zero in the middle, say 零 (líng) and don't say a unit for it (305 = 三百零五). However many zeros there are in a row in the middle, say 零 only once (1008 = 一千零八). Zeros at the end aren't said at all (1100 = 一千一百, not 一千一百零零).
Two: 二 (èr) is the digit used when counting and inside numbers (十二, 二十, 一百二十). Before 千 use 两 (liǎng): 两千. Before 百 both 二百 and 两百 are fine.
After 百 or 千, the ten is said as 一十 (yīshí), not just 十: 110 = 一百一十, 1019 = 一千零一十九. In casual speech a round number can drop its last unit: 一百五 always means 150 (105 would be 一百零五).

patterns.label: Numbers from 100 to 9,999
examples: 110、111……199 一百一十、一百一十一……一百九十九
210、211……299 二百一十、二百一十一……二百九十九
910、911……999 九百一十、九百一十一……九百九十九

patterns.label: Zero in the middle
patterns.formula: … 百/千 + 零 + digit(s)  (one 零 only)

patterns.label: “2” before units
patterns.formula: 两 + 千  ·  二百 / 两百

examples.zh: 一共两千一百九十一块。
examples.es: That's 2,191 kuai altogether.
Wrong: before 千, “2” is said 两: 两千一百九十一.
Wrong: only one 零, however many zeros: 一千零八.
Wrong: 1100 has no zero in the middle to read: 一千一百.
Wrong: for 305 you need 零: 三百零五 (三百五 means 350).

notes: Note: When “2” comes before “qiān 千”, it is read as “liǎng 两”.
Phone and room numbers are read digit by digit, and 1 is often said yāo: 110 = yāo yāo líng.
The number table and the 两千 note come from your textbook (Básico 2, p. 81); the rules about 零, 一十 and 二/两 come from the Wiki.

point: 能愿动词(1)：想、可以 · Auxiliaries 想 / 可以
title: 2. 能愿动词谓语句（1）：想、可以 Sentences with modal verbs (1): “xiǎng 想” (would like to) or “kěyǐ 可以” (can, may)
explanation: Modal verbs such as “想”, “可以”, “yào 要” (to want), “néng 能” (can), and “yīnggāi 应该” (should) are often placed before a verb, expressing intention, possibility or ability. The word “想” expresses one's subjective intention or hope. Its negative form is “bù xiǎng不想”.
The word “可以” often expresses objective conditions that allow or prohibit someone from doing something. The negative form is “不可以” (may not).

patterns.label: 想 (Affirmative / Question / Negative)
patterns.formula: Subject + 想 / 想不想 / 不想 + Verb + Object
examples: 丁力波想买一件绿色的羽绒服。
林娜想不想看北京的胡同？

patterns.label: 可以 (Affirmative / Question / Negative)
patterns.formula: Subject + 可以 / 可以不可以 / 不能 / 不可以 + Verb + Object
examples: 您可以给我介绍一下吗？
我可以不可以试一下这件衣服？
现在不能 / 不可以过马路。

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng bu xiǎng kàn diànyǐng?
examples.es: Would you like to see a movie?

examples.pinyin: Lín Nà xiǎng bu xiǎng liànxí kǒuyǔ?
examples.es: Does Lin Na want to practice spoken Chinese?
Can I pay by credit/debit card?
Yes, you can.

notes: Notes ❶ In a sentence with a modal verb, the affirmative-negative (verb/adjective-not-verb/adjective) question applies to the modal verb rather than to the action verb. For example, (1) 你想不想看电影？ Would you like to see a movie? (2) 林娜想不想练习口语？ Does Lin Na want to practice spoken Chinese?
Notes ❷ To give a short answer to a question, one can say just the modal verb. For example, A: 可以刷卡吗？ Can I pay by credit/debit card? B: 可以。 Yes, you can.
Notes ❸ Some modal verbs are also simply verbs, such as “想” in “xiǎng wèntí 想问题” (to think about a question/problem) and “xiǎng yǔfǎ 想语法” (to think about grammar).

point: 双宾语动词(2)：给、问、找 · Double objects
title: 3. 双宾语动词谓语句（2）：给、问、找 Sentences with a double-object verbal predicate (2): “gěi 给” (to give), “wèn 问” (to ask), and “zhǎo 找” (to give change)
explanation: The verbs “给”, “问” and “找” can be followed by two objects, of which the first indicates the recipient and the second indicates the thing given.

patterns.label: Subject + Verb + Object₁ + Object₂
examples: 妈妈给儿子一盒巧克力。
马大为问老板一个问题。

examples.zh: 妈妈给儿子一盒巧克力。
马大为问老板一个问题。

point: 用疑问代词的问句(3)：怎么 · 怎么 + verb
title: 4. 用疑问代词的问句（3）：怎么 Questions with interrogative pronouns (3): “zěnme 怎么” (how)
explanation: The interrogative pronoun “怎么” placed before a verb forms a question. The pattern “怎么 + verb” is often used to ask about a certain action or about how something is done, as in “zěnme shuō 怎么说” (how do you say it), “zěnme zuò 怎么做” (how do you do it), “zěnme qù 怎么去” (how do you get there), “zěnme xiě 怎么写” (how do you write it), among others.
notes: Note: In this type of sentence, the subject is often the receiver of the action, but it is also the topic of the comment.

title: ③ 苹果多少钱一斤？ How much is half a kilo of apples?
explanation: “……duōshao qián yì jīn? 多少钱一斤？” (How much is half a kilo of...?) is a common expression used to ask the price of something when shopping. The jin is the most commonly used unit of weight in China. One jin is equivalent to half a kilogram. The legal measure stipulated by the Chinese government is the “qiānkè 千克” (1,000 grams) or “gōngjīn 公斤” (kilogram), but in everyday life people just use the word jin.

examples.es: How much is half a kilo of apples?
Five kuai (yuan) fifty a jin.

notes: Note ① (p. 80) 这件衬衫多少钱？ How much is this shirt?: The question “Zhè jiàn chènshān duōshao qián? 这件衬衫多少钱？” and the answer “(Zhè jiàn chènshān 这件衬衫) 399 kuài 块。” are sentences with a nominal predicate. The predicate can be an interrogative pronoun, a number-measure word compound or a noun phrase. In addition to age, time and dates, which we have learned before, a sentence with a nominal predicate can also express a price, an amount of money, etc.

title: ④ 五块五一斤。 Five kuai (yuan) fifty a jin.
explanation: The currency in circulation in China is the “rénmínbì 人民币” (literally, the people's currency). The units of the currency are the “yuán 元”, the “jiǎo 角” (one tenth of a “元”) and the “fēn 分” (one hundredth of a “元”). In spoken Chinese, people usually say “kuài 块” and “máo 毛” instead of the written forms “元” and “角”. When “毛” or “分” comes at the end, it can be omitted. For example,

patterns.label: Written → spoken
patterns.formula: 元 / 角 / 分 → 块 / 毛 / 分 (final 毛 or 分 can be omitted)
examples: 1.75 元 → 一块七毛五（分钱）

examples.zh: 1.75 元 → 一块七毛五（分钱）
examples.pinyin: 1.75 yuán → yí kuài qī máo wǔ (fēn qián)

notes: Note: When an amount of money begins with the number “2”, one says “liǎng 两”. For example, 2.20 元 → 两块二; 0.22 元 → 两毛二.

title: 形容词 + (一)点儿 · “a bit more …”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Comparing "youdian" and "yidian"” — not from the textbook
explanation: When (一)点儿 comes AFTER an adjective, it means “a little more …”: 便宜一点儿 = a bit cheaper. It's used to ask for something (a request), to say what you'd like, or to compare.
In this position 一 is usually dropped, so you'll often hear just 便宜点儿吧! Adding 吧 makes the request softer and more polite — a typical way to bargain.

Don't put 一点儿 BEFORE an adjective. To say “a bit (too) …” about something you don't like, Chinese uses 有点儿 + adjective instead (今天有点儿热), which you'll meet in L8. Easy rule: 有点儿 goes before the adjective and complains; 一点儿 goes after it and asks for more.

patterns.label: Do something in a certain way
Shopping: a … -er one
patterns.formula: 有没有 + Adj + 一点儿 + 的？

examples.es: A bit cheaper, please!
Please speak a bit more slowly.
A bit faster! / Hurry up!
Do you have a slightly bigger one?
Wrong: 一点儿 goes after the adjective: 便宜一点儿吧.
Wrong: to complain “a bit hot”, use 有点儿 before the adjective: 今天有点儿热.

notes: (一)点儿 can also come before a noun to mean “a little / some”: 喝点儿咖啡, 买点儿苹果 (your book's L7 Note ①).
Your course material doesn't explain this point: L7 Note ⑤ only translates 便宜点儿吧 without explaining the structure.

point: 双宾语(2)：给 · 给 + person + thing
title: 3. 双宾语动词谓语句（2）：给、问、找 Sentences with a double-object verbal predicate (2): “gěi 给” (to give), “wèn 问” (to ask), and “zhǎo 找” (to give change)
explanation: The verbs “给”, “问” and “找” can be followed by two objects, of which the first indicates the recipient and the second indicates the thing given.

patterns.label: Subject + Verb + Object₁ + Object₂
examples: 妈妈给儿子一盒巧克力。
马大为问老板一个问题。

examples.zh: 妈妈给儿子一盒巧克力。
马大为问老板一个问题。

title: 怎么 · “How come…?”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Asking why with "zenme"” — not from the textbook
explanation: Besides “how” (怎么 + verb = how to do something), 怎么 can mean “why / how come”. It's not a neutral question: it shows you're surprised, and sometimes that you don't like the situation.
This meaning is clearest when 怎么 is followed by 不 or 没: 你怎么不去？ “How come you're not going?” Nobody asks “in what way are you not going?”, so it must be “why”.
Without a negative, context decides. 你怎么去？ usually asks the method (“How are you getting there?”), but 你怎么来了？ said with surprise means “What are you doing here?”.
为什么 is the neutral “why”, just asking for the reason. 怎么 adds “I didn't expect this!”

patterns.label: Why not…? (surprise)
patterns.formula: Subject + 怎么 + 不/没 + Verb/Adj？

patterns.label: How can it be so…?
patterns.formula: Subject + 怎么 + 这么/那么 + Adj？

examples.es: How come you're not going?
How come he still isn't here?

examples.zh: 今天是星期一，你怎么不上课？
examples.pinyin: Jīntiān shì xīngqīyī, nǐ zěnme bú shàng kè?
examples.es: It's Monday — why aren't you going to class?
How can it be so cold today?
How are you getting there? (method, not “why”)
Wrong: 怎么 is already a question word, so no 吗.

notes: 怎么了？ on its own means “What's wrong? / What happened?”.
Your course material doesn't explain this point: L4–7 only explain 怎么 + verb = “how” (Grammar 4).

title: 1. 主谓谓语句 Sentences with a subject-predicate phrase as predicate
explanation: This type of sentence, at the first level, consists of a subject (subject₁) and a predicate (predicate₁). The predicate itself, at the second level, also consists of a subject (subject₂) and a predicate (predicate₂). Subject₂ within predicate₁ is often a part or an aspect of the subject (subject₁) of the whole sentence.
In the negative form, the adverb “bù 不” is placed at the second level. The affirmative-negative (verb/adjective-not-verb/adjective) question can also appear at the second level.
notes: Exercise II (p. 11): 他头疼。→ 他头不疼。→ 他头疼不疼？

point: 选择疑问句 · Questions with 还是
title: 2. 选择疑问句 Alternative questions
explanation: Alternative questions use “háishi 还是” (or) to connect option A and option B. When answering, one must choose between A and B.

patterns.label: Question / Answer
patterns.formula: Option A + 还是 + Option B？ → Answer (Option A or B)
examples: 现在去还是下午去？ — 现在去。(Option A)
内科在一层还是二层？ — 在二层。(Option B)
你是老师还是学生？ — 我是学生。(Option B)
她学习汉语还是学习英语？ — 她学习汉语。(Option A)

examples.es: (Option A)
(Option B)
(Option B)

examples.es: (Option A)

notes: Exercise I (p. 11): 我们现在去还是明天去？(现在去 / 明天去)

point: 连动句(1)：表示目的 · Serial verbs (purpose)
title: 3. 连动句（1）：表示目的 Serial verb sentences (1): Expressing purpose
explanation: In a serial verb sentence (1), the subject has two serial verbs or verb phrases as its predicate. The order of the verbs is fixed. Verb₂ explains the purpose of verb₁. The negative adverb “bù 不” is usually placed before verb₁.

patterns.label: Structure
examples: 你们明天去不去超市买苹果？

patterns.label: Table: Subject | Adverbial | Verb₁ (Object₁) | Verb₂ (Object₂)
examples: 你们明天去不去超市买苹果？

examples.zh: 你们明天去不去超市买苹果？

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bù yīnggāi qù fànguǎn chī fàn.
examples.es: You shouldn't eat at the restaurant.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bù néng zài zhèr xī yān.
examples.es: You can't smoke here.

notes: Note: When there is a modal verb in a sentence, the negative adverb “不” must be placed before the modal verb. For example, (1) 你不应该去饭馆吃饭。Nǐ bù yīnggāi qù fànguǎn chī fàn. You shouldn't eat at the restaurant. (2) 你不能在这儿吸烟。Nǐ bù néng zài zhèr xī yān. You can't smoke here.

point: 能愿动词(2)：应该、要、能 · Auxiliaries
title: 4. 能愿动词谓语句（2）：应该、要、能 Sentences with modal verbs (2): “yīnggāi 应该” (should), “yào 要” (need; want), and “néng 能” (can; be able to)
explanation: The modal verb “应该” expresses that “it is necessary to do something”.
The modal verb “要” often expresses that “something needs to be done”. The negative form is “búyòng 不用” (no need). For example,
The modal verb “能” often expresses the meaning “can; be able to”. The negative form is “bù néng 不能” (cannot; be unable to).

patterns.label: 应该 — Subject | Modal verb | Verb-Object
patterns.formula: Subject + 应该 / 不应该 + Verb-Object
examples: 马大为应该去医院看病。
你不应该买那件很贵的衬衫。

patterns.label: 要 — Subject | Modal verb | Verb-Object
patterns.formula: Subject + 要 / 不用 / 要不要 + Verb-Object
examples: 我要给他女儿买礼物吗？
你要给她买点儿巧克力。

patterns.label: 能 — Subject | Adverbial | Modal verb | Verb-Object
examples: 小云星期六能参加聚会吗？

examples.zh: 马大为应该去医院看病。
你不应该买那件很贵的衬衫。
我要给他女儿买礼物吗？
你要给她买点儿巧克力。
小云星期六能参加聚会吗？

notes: Exercise (p. 14): 他要打针。→ 他不用打针。→ 他要不要打针？
Exercise (p. 14): 应该 你 休息 多 → 你应该多休息。

point: 介词结构(2)：在 + place · 在 + place + verb
title: 5. 介词结构（2）：在 + 代词/名词 Prepositional constructions (2): “zài 在” (in, at) + Pronoun/Noun
explanation: The word “在” is a verb and also a preposition. The preposition “在” followed by a noun or a phrase, which is usually a place word, forms a prepositional construction. It is placed before the verbal predicate, indicating the place where the action takes place.

patterns.label: Subject | Preposition 在 + Pronoun/Noun | Verb/Verb phrase
patterns.formula: Subject + (不) 在 + Pronoun/Noun + Verb/Verb phrase
examples: 张老师不在我们班上课。

examples.zh: 张老师不在我们班上课。

notes: Exercise (p. 16): A: 你在哪儿工作？ B: 我在北京工作。

title: ① 快起床！ Get up, quick!
explanation: “kuài 快 + verb (phrase)” is used to hurry someone to do something, as in “kuài lái 快来” (come quickly) and “kuài shuō 快说” (say it, quick).

examples.es: Get up, quick!
come quickly
say it, quick

title: ② 你每天早上都六点去运动。 You go exercise at six o'clock every morning.
explanation: When “měi 每” modifies a noun, it generally requires a measure word, as in “měi gè xuésheng 每个学生” (every student) and “měi jīn píngguǒ 每斤苹果” (every jin of apples).
However, when “每” modifies “tiān 天” (day) or “nián 年” (year), it cannot take a measure word, for example, “měi tiān 每天” (every day) and “měi nián 每年” (every year).

When “每” modifies “yuè 月” (month) or “xīngqī 星期” (week), it can appear with or without a measure word, as in “měi gè yuè 每个月” or “měi yuè 每月” (every month), or “měi gè xīngqī 每个星期” or “měi xīngqī 每星期” (every week).
The word “每” is often used with “dōu 都” (both; all). For example,

patterns.label: Structure
patterns.formula: 每 + (measure word) + noun + 都 + verb

examples.pinyin: Tā měi tiān dōu qù túshūguǎn.
examples.es: He goes to the library every day.

examples.pinyin: Tā měi gè yuè dōu huí jiā.
examples.es: She goes back home every month.

title: ③ 今天为什么九点还不起床？ It's already nine; why haven't you gotten up yet today?
explanation: The adverb “hái 还” (still), apart from the meaning “in addition”, is often placed before an adjective or a verb to express a continuing state. For example,

patterns.label: Structure
patterns.formula: 还 + (不 / 没有 / 是) + adjective / verb
examples: 我哥哥现在还没有孩子。

examples.zh: 晚上十二点她不睡觉，一点她还不睡觉。
examples.pinyin: Wǎnshang shí'èr diǎn tā bú shuìjiào, yī diǎn tā hái bú shuìjiào.
examples.es: She didn't go to bed at 12 midnight, and at one she still isn't going to bed.

examples.zh: 他爸爸很忙，星期天还工作。
examples.pinyin: Tā bàba hěn máng, Xīngqītiān hái gōngzuò.
examples.es: His father is very busy and still works on Sunday.

examples.zh: 我哥哥现在还没有孩子。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ gēge xiànzài hái méiyǒu háizi.
examples.es: As of today, my older brother still doesn't have a child.

examples.zh: 昨天很冷，今天还是很冷。
examples.pinyin: Zuótiān hěn lěng, jīntiān háishi hěn lěng.
examples.es: It was cold yesterday, and it's still cold today.

notes: Note: When “还” is placed before an adjective, it is often followed by “shì 是”, as shown in example (4) above. The negative adverb “bù 不” or the verb “yǒu 有 / méiyǒu 没有” must be placed after “还”, as we see in examples (1) and (3) above.

An interrogative sentence with the interrogative pronoun “wèi shénme 为什么” is often used to ask the reason for something. For example, (1) 马大为为什么不来上课？ Mǎ Dàwéi wèi shénme bù lái shàngkè? Why hasn't Ma Dawei come to class? —他头疼。Tā tóu téng. – He has a headache. (2) 林娜为什么不去看电影？ Lín Nà wèi shénme bú qù kàn diànyǐng? Why didn't Lin Na go to see the movie? —她特别忙。Tā tèbié máng. – She was very busy.

point: Notes L8 · 有点儿 / 一点儿
title: ⑤ 我嗓子也有点儿疼。 My throat also hurts a little.
explanation: When “yǒu (yì) diǎnr 有（一）点儿” (“一” is often omitted) is placed before an adjective or verb as an adverbial modifier, it expresses a certain degree. When it is before an adjective, it often has a negative or dissatisfied connotation. For example, “yǒudiǎnr bù gāoxìng 有点儿不高兴” (to be a bit unhappy), and “yǒudiǎnr lèi 有点儿累” (to be a bit tired).

Note: The uses of “yǒu yìdiǎnr 有一点儿” and “yìdiǎnr 一点儿” are different. “有一点儿” is used as an adverbial modifier that modifies an adjective or a verb. “一点儿” is used as a modifier of a noun. For example, “yìdiǎnr cǎoméi 一点儿草莓” (some strawberries), “yìdiǎnr qián 一点儿钱” (a little money), and “yìdiǎnr yào 一点儿药” (some medicine). “一点儿 + noun” is often placed after a verb and acts as the object. For example, “Wǒ qù mǎi yìdiǎnr dōngxi. 我去买一点儿东西。” (I'm going to buy some things.) “一点儿” cannot replace “有一点儿”. For example,

examples.es: He is a bit unhappy. (We cannot say “* 他一点儿不高兴。”)
I have a slight headache. (We cannot say “* 我一点儿头疼。”)
I'm going to buy some things.

notes: We cannot say “* 他一点儿不高兴。” or “* 我一点儿头疼。”

title: ⑦ 我跟你一起去。 I'll go with you.
explanation: When the prepositional construction “gēn 跟 + pronoun/noun phrase” is placed before a verb as an adverbial modifier, it is often used with “yìqǐ 一起” (together). “跟 + pronoun/noun phrase + 一起 + verb phrase” expresses the meaning of doing something with someone. For example,

patterns.label: Structure
patterns.formula: 跟 + pronoun/noun phrase + 一起 + verb phrase
examples: 力波跟大为一起去医院。
林娜跟宋华一起练习口语。

examples.zh: 力波跟大为一起去医院。
examples.pinyin: Lìbō gēn Dàwéi yìqǐ qù yīyuàn.
examples.es: Libo went to the hospital with Dawei.

examples.zh: 林娜跟宋华一起练习口语。
examples.pinyin: Lín Nà gēn Sòng Huá yìqǐ liànxí kǒuyǔ.
examples.es: Lin Na practiced spoken Chinese with Song Hua.

point: Notes L8 · 一点儿也不 + adj
title: 一点儿也不 + 形容词 · “not … at all”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing "not at all" with "yidianr ye bu"” — not from the textbook
explanation: To say “not at all” / “not the least bit”, put 一点儿也不 (or 一点儿都不) before an adjective: 一点儿也不贵 “not expensive at all”. 也 and 都 mean the same here.
All four pieces are needed, in this order: 一点儿 + 也/都 + 不 + adjective. Without 也/都 the sentence is wrong (your book warns that 他一点儿不高兴 is incorrect).
It also works with verbs of feeling or knowing, like 喜欢 or 知道: 我一点儿也不喜欢. For something that didn't happen in the past, use 没 instead of 不: 我一点儿也没吃.
Don't confuse it with 有点儿 + adjective (“a bit too…”): 有点儿贵 = a bit expensive; 一点儿也不贵 = not expensive at all.

patterns.label: Not … at all (adjective)
patterns.formula: Subject + 一点儿 + 也/都 + 不 + Adj
examples: 这件衣服一点儿也不贵。

patterns.label: With verbs
patterns.formula: Subject + 一点儿 + 也/都 + 不 + Verb (+ Obj)

patterns.label: Past: didn't … at all
patterns.formula: Subject + 一点儿 + 也/都 + 没 + Verb

examples.es: It's not expensive at all.

examples.pinyin: Zhège cài yìdiǎnr dōu bú là.
examples.es: This dish isn't spicy at all.

examples.zh: 汉语语法一点儿也不难。
examples.pinyin: Hànyǔ yǔfǎ yìdiǎnr yě bù nán.
examples.es: Chinese grammar isn't hard at all.
I'm not tired at all.
I didn't eat anything at all.
Wrong: you need 也 or 都: 一点儿也不贵.
Wrong: the order is 一点儿 + 也/都 + 不 + adjective.

notes: This pattern is negative only: you can't say ✗ 一点儿也很贵.
Your course material doesn't explain this point: L8 Note ⑤ only contrasts 有（一）点儿 + adjective with 一点儿 + noun.

point: 句尾“了”(1)：变化 · 了 for change of state
title: 1. 助词“了”在句尾（1）：表示情况的变化 The particle “le 了” at the end of a sentence (1): Expressing a change of state
explanation: The particle “了” at the end of a sentence expresses a change of state or a new situation. This use often appears in a sentence with an adjective or a noun as the predicate, as well as in a sentence with the verb “shì 是” (to be) or “yǒu 有” (to have; there is), etc.

To find out whether the state has changed or not, we often use a question ending in “吗”. If the state has not changed, we often use “méiyǒu 没有” (see the first, second and fourth sentences above). If the sentence contains the verb “是”, the negative answer is “bú shì 不是” (see the third sentence above).

patterns.label: Declarative sentence
examples: 天气凉快了。(It was hot before.)
树都绿了。(They weren't green before.)
现在是秋天了。(It was summer before.)
今天我（也）有时间了。(I didn't have time before.)

patterns.label: Question ending in “ma 吗” (To find out whether the state has changed or not)
Negative sentence (The state has not changed)

examples.es: (It was hot before.)
(They weren't green before.)
(It was summer before.)
(I didn't have time before.)

notes: Exercise (p. 36–37): A: 你累不累？ B: 我累了，我想休息。 / A: 现在是秋天了。 B: 是啊，天气凉快了。 / A: 现在几点了？ B: 七点了，你快起床吧。

point: 连动句(2)：表示方式 · Serial verbs (means)
title: 2. 连动句（2）：表示方式 Sentences with serial verb phrases (2): Expressing means or manner
explanation: In Lesson 8, we learned sentences with serial verb phrases (1): expressing purpose.
In this lesson, the first verb of the sentence with serial verb phrases generally expresses the means or manner of the second verb. For example,

patterns.label: Structure
examples: 他每天坐公共汽车回家。

examples.zh: 他每天坐公共汽车回家。
examples.pinyin: Tā měi tiān zuò gōnggòng qìchē huí jiā.
examples.es: He goes home by bus every day.
We went to Wangfujing by car.

examples.pinyin: Dàwéi kěyǐ yóu(yǒng) huí guó ma?
examples.es: Can Dawei swim back to his country?

notes: Exercise I (p. 38), Example: 我常常坐飞机去上海。

point: 能愿动词(3)：会、可能 · Auxiliaries 会 / 可能
title: 3. 能愿动词谓语句（3）：会、可能 Sentences with auxiliary verbs (3): “huì 会” (can; to be able to) and “kěnéng 可能” (to be possible)
explanation: The auxiliary verb “会” is often used before a verb to express an ability that can be acquired through study or practice. For example, “huì kāichē 会开车” (can drive), “huì yóuyǒng 会游泳” (can swim), and “huì shuō Hànyǔ 会说汉语” (can speak Chinese).
The auxiliary verb “可能” expresses “possibility” and is usually an estimate with uncertainty.

patterns.label: 会 — Subject | Auxiliary verb | Verb-Object
patterns.formula: Subject + 会 / 不会 / 会不会 + Verb-Object

patterns.label: 可能 — Subject | Time word | Auxiliary verb | Verb-Object/Adjective
patterns.formula: Subject + (Time word) + 可能 / 不可能 + Verb-Object/Adjective
examples: 陆雨平八月可能去上海。
马大为现在不可能睡觉。
王小云明天可能来学校吗？

can swim

point: 疑问代词(4)：怎么样 · Suggestions with 怎么样
title: 4. 用疑问代词的问句（4）：怎么样 Questions with an interrogative pronoun (4): “zěnmeyàng 怎么样” (What is it/are they like...? / How about...?)
explanation: The use of “……，怎么样” is similar to the use of “……，hǎo ma 好吗？” at the end of a sentence. It is often used to make a suggestion or to ask for other people's opinions. The first half of the sentence is a statement expressing a suggestion. For example,

The affirmative answer is often “hǎo a 好啊”, “hǎo 好”, “hǎo de 好的”, “hǎo ba 好吧”, or “tài hǎo le 太好了”, etc.; the negative answer can be “bùxíng 不行” (no) or “zhēn bù hǎoyìsi 真不好意思，……” (I'm really sorry), or “duìbuqǐ 对不起，……” (sorry), etc., explaining the reason for this answer.

patterns.label: Structure
examples: 我们买一个大蛋糕，怎么样？

examples.zh: 我们买一个大蛋糕，怎么样？
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen mǎi yí gè dà dàngāo, zěnmeyàng?

How about we go now?

title: ④ 可是（飞）机票太贵了。 But the plane ticket is too expensive.
explanation: “tài 太 + adjective + le 了” indicates that the degree of the adjective is very high and even exceeds the ordinary. If the nature of the adjective is negative, as in “tài guì le 太贵了” or “tài rè le 太热了”, it expresses a feeling of excess and dissatisfaction. If the nature of the adjective is positive, as in “tài hǎo le 太好了” or “tài piàoliang le 太漂亮了”, it expresses satisfaction and exclamation.

examples.es: But the plane ticket is too expensive.

title: 快……了 · “almost / about to”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing "about to happen" with "le"” — not from the textbook
explanation: 快……了 says that something is about to happen or that we're almost at a point: 快十点了 “It's almost ten o'clock.” Here 了 doesn't mean the past — it marks a change that's coming soon.
Between 快 and 了 you can put a verb (快到了 “almost there”), an adjective (天快黑了 “it's getting dark”), or a time/number phrase (快十点了, 他快二十岁了).
快要……了 means the same. 要……了 (without 快) also means “about to”: 火车要开了 “The train is about to leave.”
Both 快 and 了 are needed: 快十点 alone is incomplete.

examples.es: It's almost ten o'clock.
We're almost there.
It's about to rain.
It's getting dark.

examples.pinyin: Tā kuài yào èrshí suì le.
examples.es: He's almost twenty.
Wrong: you need 了 at the end: 快十点了.
Wrong: 快 comes before what is approaching: 快十点了.

notes: Because 快 already means “soon”, avoid putting an exact future time like 明天 in front of 快……了; with a specific time, use 就要……了 instead (他明天就要来了).
Your course material doesn't explain this point: L9 Note ② only translates 快十点了 (“It's almost 10 o'clock now”).

title: ② 秋天是北京最好的季节。 Autumn is the best season in Beijing.
explanation: “zuì 最 + adjective” expresses the idea that someone or something surpasses all others of the same category. For example, “Zuótiān zuì rè. 昨天最热。” (Yesterday was the hottest day.) “Tā shì wǒ zuì xiǎo de dìdi. 他是我最小的弟弟。” (He is my youngest brother.) “最” can also be used before verbs of feeling and desire to express the superlative degree. For example,

examples: 林娜最想看北京的胡同。

examples.es: What Lin Na would like most is to see a hutong in Beijing.

title: 会 · “will / be likely to”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing "will" with "hui"” — not from the textbook
explanation: You know 会 as “can / know how to” for skills learned by practice (我会说汉语). 会 has a second use: before a verb, it predicts that something will (probably) happen — “will / be likely to”.
It's common with the weather, plans and guesses about other people: 明天会下雨吗？ “Will it rain tomorrow?” 他会来 “He'll come.”
The negative is 不会: 他今天不会来 “He won't come today.” To answer a 会 question, just say 会 or 不会.
Compare 可能: 可能 = “maybe / possibly” (less sure); 会 = “will” (you expect it). They can combine: 明天可能会下雨 “It may rain tomorrow.”

patterns.label: Question / negative
patterns.formula: Subject + 会 + Verb + 吗？  ·  Subject + 不会 + Verb

examples.es: Will it rain tomorrow?
Will he come? — Yes, he will.
He won't come today.
It's going to be cold tomorrow.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ huì gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
examples.es: I'll call you.
Wrong: 会 goes before the verb: 明天会下雨吗？
Wrong: a 会 prediction doesn't take 了: 明天会下雨.

notes: The same sentence can be ambiguous only in theory: 他会来 is “he'll come”, while 他会开车 is “he can drive” — the verb and context make it clear.
Your course material doesn't explain this point: L9 Grammar 3 only presents 会 as an ability learned through study or practice, and uses 可能 for possibility.

point: 句尾“了”(2)：已经发生 · 了 for something that has happened
title: 1. 助词“了”在句尾（2）：肯定事情的发生或实现 The particle “le 了” at the end of a sentence (2): Confirming that something has happened
explanation: In a sentence with a verbal predicate denoting an action or behavior, the particle “了” is often used to confirm that something has happened or has been completed. Compare the questions and answers in A (without “了”) and in B (with “了”):
In dialogue A, the two actions “去王府井” and “买圣诞节礼物” have not happened; in dialogue B, the two actions have happened.
The negative form of a sentence with the particle “了” is made by adding the adverb “méi (yǒu) 没（有）” (instead of “bù 不”) before the verb, and “了” must be removed. See example 3 in the table below.

To ask a question, “……吗” or “……没有” is added at the end of the sentence, as we see in examples 4 and 5 in the table below. The “verb + 没 + verb” pattern can also be used to ask this type of question, as in the last example in the table below.

patterns.label: Verb + Object + 了 (Subject | Adverbial modifier | Verb | Object | Auxiliary particle)
examples: 你给妈妈打电话了没有？
林娜和宋华看没看展览？

examples.es: Where are you going?
I'm going to Wangfujing.
What are you going to buy?

examples.es: I'm going to buy a Christmas present.
Where did you go?/Where have you been?
I went to Wangfujing./I've been to Wangfujing.
What did you buy?/What have you bought?

examples.zh: 你给妈妈打电话了没有？

notes: Note: The particle “了” always denotes that an action or something has occurred in the past. However, something that occurred in the past does not necessarily require “了”. It is not necessary to use “了” if it is a general statement that does not emphasize confirming what has happened, particularly when a series of actions is mentioned or a description is given of something that happened at a particular time. For example, (1) 上星期六他上午去看电影，下午去参加一个聚会。Shàng Xīngqīliù tā shàngwǔ qù kàn diànyǐng, xiàwǔ qù cānjiā yí gè jùhuì. Last Saturday, he went to see a movie in the morning and attended a party in the afternoon. (2) 他以前也在语言学院学汉语。Tā yǐqián yě zài Yǔyán Xuéyuàn xué Hànyǔ. point: 兼语句 · Pivotal sentences (请 / 让)
title: 2. 兼语句 Pivotal sentences
explanation: A pivotal sentence is also a sentence with a verbal predicate. Its predicate is made up of two verb phrases. The object of the first verb is also the subject of the second verb. The first verb in a pivotal sentence is often a verb meaning to ask or order someone to do something, such as “qǐng 请” (to ask/to invite) or “ràng 让” (to allow/to let/to tell/to ask/to make).
Both “请” and “让” can mean “to ask someone to do something”, but “请” is a more polite way of making a request.

Both verbs in the predicate of a pivotal sentence can take an adverbial modifier. The negative sentence is generally formed by adding “bù 不” or “méi (yǒu) 没（有）” before the first verb. To form a question, you add “…… ma 吗？”, “…… le ma 了吗？”, or “…… le méiyǒu 了没有？” at the end, or use the “verb-not-verb” pattern with the first verb.

patterns.label: Subject₁ | Verb₁ | Object₁ (Subject₂) | Verb₂ | Object₂
patterns.formula: Subject₁ + Verb₁ (请/让) + Object₁ (Subject₂) + Verb₂ + Object₂
examples: 你哥哥昨天让你给妈妈打电话。
他爱人让他买圣诞礼物了吗？
他们请她唱中国歌了没有？
妈妈让不让小女儿喝咖啡？

title: 1.情态补语（1）The modal complement
explanation: In Chinese, after some verbs and adjectives, there are often certain additional comments called 补语（complement）.
There are many types of complements. The one that describes or comments on the state of the action or behavior is known as the “modal complement”.
The modal complement is generally formed by an adjective or an adjective phrase. The structural particle “得” must be used to connect the verb and the modal complement.
If the verb takes an object, the verb is repeated after the object, followed by “得” and a modal complement. The first verb is often omitted.

patterns.label: Affirmative
patterns.formula: S + V + 得 + modal complement(adv +adj)  ·  V + 得 + Adv. + Adj.

title: 刚 / 刚才 · “just” vs. “just now”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Comparing 刚 and 刚才” — not from the textbook
explanation: Both translate as “just”, but they are different parts of speech. 刚 (gāng) is an adverb: it always goes directly before the verb (or adjective). 刚才 (gāngcái) is a time word, like 今天 or 现在: it can go before or after the subject.
刚才 means “a moment ago” in absolute terms — minutes, not days. 刚 means “only just”, relative to the speaker's point of view, so it also works for something that happened yesterday or even last year.
Because 刚才 points to a moment in the past, a completed action usually takes 了 (刚才我听错了). With 刚, 了 is usually left out (我刚到).
Only 刚才 can be negated with 没 or modify a noun with 的. Only 刚 can be followed by a duration (我刚来北京两个月, “I've only been in Beijing for two months”) or by an adjective.

patterns.formula: 刚才 + Subject + Verb + 了  ·  Subject + 刚才 + Verb + 了
examples: 刚才银行人少，不用排队。

patterns.formula: 刚才 + 没 + Verb  ·  刚才 + 的 + Noun

title: 次 · Counting how many times (verbal measure word)
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Measure words for verbs” and “Comparing "bian" and "ci"” (AllSet Vocabulary Wiki) — not from the textbook
explanation: Nouns have measure words (一本书), and so do actions. 次 (cì) is the basic measure word for verbs: it counts how many times something happens. Unlike English “twice / three times”, which can go at the end of the sentence, number + 次 comes right after the verb (and after 了 or 过 if there is one).

If the verb has an ordinary noun object, number + 次 usually goes between the verb and the object: 我看过三次这个电影. With a place name you can say it either way: 去了两次上海 or 去了上海两次. With a pronoun object (我、你、他…), the pronoun comes first: 我见过他两次.
次 can also work like a noun measure word for “occasion”: 这次 (this time), 上次 (last time), 下次 (next time), 第一次 (the first time). And to say how often, put the time period first: 一天三次, 一个星期两次.
次 vs. 遍 (biàn): 次 just counts occurrences. 遍 stresses doing the whole thing from beginning to end — reading a whole book, listening to a whole song, saying a whole sentence again (再说一遍).

point: Usage L11 · 离合词 · Separable verbs
title: 离合词 · Separable verbs (排队, 睡觉, 换钱…)
source: Lesson 11 A (slides), p. 8 (排队); general rules from the Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Separable verb” — not from the textbook
explanation: 排队 páiduì (to stand in line) is a verb-object (VO) word: 排 v. to arrange / put in order + 队 n. line / team. (Slides)

Many common verbs are built the same way and are called separable verbs (离合词): 睡觉 (sleep), 吃饭 (eat), 上课 (have class), 换钱 (change money), 看病 (see a doctor), 生病 (fall ill), 唱歌 (sing), 游泳 (swim), 见面 (meet). They can be used as one word (我要排队), but other words often go between the verb and its object.

了 / 过 go after the verb part, not after the whole word: 我换了钱, 我们见过面. A duration or a number of times also goes in the middle: 我排了一个小时队, 我只睡了五个小时觉, 我看了两次病. Another way is to repeat the verb: 我排队排了一个小时.
A separable verb already has its object, so it can’t take another one after it: say 跟他见面 (meet him), not 见面他. 一下 can’t follow the whole word either; repeat the verb part instead: 见见面, 帮帮忙.

explanation: The resultative complement indicates the result of an action. This complement can be a verb or an adjective.
The resultative complement and the verb are closely linked, with no other word between them. The particle “了” or the object must be placed after the resultative complement.

title: 把 · The 把 construction
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Using "ba" sentences” — not from the textbook
explanation: A 把 sentence moves the object in front of the verb: Subject + 把 + Object + Verb + something more. You use it to say what you do to a specific thing and how it ends up — where you put it, who you give it to, whether it's finished, broken, done wrong…

Two conditions: (1) the object must be something specific that both speakers know about (那本书, 我的护照, 姓名), not “a book” in general; (2) the verb can't stand alone — something must follow it: 在 + place, 给 + person, a result complement (完、好、错、干净…), a direction (来/去) or at least 了.
Negation and modal words go before 把, never inside: 我没把护照带来, 别把书放在这儿.

Only verbs that actually do something to the object work with 把. Verbs of feeling, knowing or being — 喜欢、爱、想、知道、觉得、是、有、在 — don't, because nothing happens to the object. Use a normal sentence instead: 我喜欢这个电影.

title: 才 / 就 · Later vs. earlier than expected
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Comparing "cai" and "jiu"” (also “Expressing lateness with "cai"” and “Expressing earliness with "jiu"”) — not from the textbook
explanation: 才 (cái) and 就 (jiù) are adverbs that go right before the verb, after a time word. They add the speaker's feeling about the timing: 才 = later (or harder, slower) than expected — “not until”; 就 = earlier (or easier, quicker) than expected — “already, as early as”.
The time expression always comes before 才/就: 他八点才起床 (he didn't get up until eight), 他六点就起床了 (he was already up at six). It can be a clock time, an age, or a period: 两个星期以后才…, 十分钟就….
Watch 了: with 才 the action is felt as having only just happened, so the verb does NOT take 了 (他八点才起床). With 就 for something in the past, the sentence usually ends in 了 (他六点就起床了).
就 can also mean “very soon” for the future: 他们一会儿就到 (they'll be here in a moment). And 才 alone can mean the speaker thinks you're late: 你怎么才来？

point: 时量补语 · Complement of duration (inferred)
title: 时量补语 · How long an action lasts (duration complement)
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing duration with "le"” (also “Separable verb” and “Expressing duration”) — not from the textbook
explanation: To say how long an action lasted, put the duration AFTER the verb, normally with 了 for a finished action: 我等了五十分钟. This is the opposite of a point in time (八点, 昨天), which goes BEFORE the verb.

With a noun object there are two options. (1) Duration between the verb and the object, optionally with 的: 他学了一年(的)汉语. (2) Say the verb with its object, then repeat the verb with the duration: 你今天坐火车坐了多长时间？
Separable verbs (睡觉、上课、见面、开会…) are already verb + object, so the duration goes in the middle: 睡了两个小时(的)觉 — or repeat the verb: 睡觉睡了两个小时.

If the object is a pronoun (我、你、他…), it stays right after the verb and the duration comes after it: 我等了你五十分钟. Adding a second 了 at the end means the action is still going on: 他在北京住了两年了 (and still lives there).

patterns.label: Noun object
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + 了 + Duration + (的) + Object

patterns.label: Repeat the verb
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + Object + Verb + 了 + Duration
examples: 你今天坐火车坐了多长时间？

patterns.label: Separable verb
patterns.formula: Subject + V + 了 + Duration + (的) + O
examples: 我们上了三个小时(的)课。

patterns.label: Still going on
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + 了 + Duration + 了

examples.zh: 你今天坐火车坐了多长时间？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān zuò huǒchē zuò le duō cháng shíjiān?
examples.es: How long were you on the train today?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shuì le liǎng ge xiǎoshí jiào.
examples.es: I slept for two hours.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ děng le nǐ wǔshí fēnzhōng.
examples.es: I waited for you for fifty minutes.

examples.pinyin: Tā xué le yì nián Hànyǔ.
examples.es: He studied Chinese for a year.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài Běijīng zhù le liǎng nián le.
examples.es: He has been living in Beijing for two years (and still does).
Wrong: the duration goes after the verb: 我睡了两个小时（的）觉。
Wrong: with a separable verb, put the duration inside (睡了两个小时觉) or repeat the verb (睡觉睡了两个小时).
Wrong: a pronoun object comes before the duration: 我等了你五十分钟。

notes: Ask “how long” with 多长时间 or 多久 in the duration slot: 你等了多长时间？
For “haven't done it for…”, the duration goes first: 我两天没睡觉了 (see “Expressing duration of inaction” on the Grammar Wiki).
The pronoun-object order (我等了你五十分钟) and verb repetition (坐火车坐了…) are standard rules not spelled out in the Wiki articles used.

title: 一会儿 · A little while
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing duration with "le"” (also “Expressing "again" in the future with "zai"” and “Expressing earliness with "jiu"”) — not from the textbook
explanation: 一会儿 (yíhuìr) means “a little while, a moment”. Used as a duration it behaves like 两个小时 or 五分钟: it goes after the verb (with 了 for a finished action), and before a noun object: 我听了一会儿音乐.
With 再 it means “a bit longer”: 再等一会儿 (wait a little longer), 再聊一会儿吧. Don't combine this with a reduplicated verb (not ✗ 再等等一会儿).
Placed before the verb, 一会儿 is a time word meaning “in a moment, soon”, often followed by 就: 他们一会儿就到. 一会儿见 means “see you in a bit”.
Don't confuse it with 一下 (yíxià), which makes an action brief or casual (看一下, 等一下). 一会儿 talks about an amount of time.

patterns.label: For a little while
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + 了 + 一会儿 (+ Object)

examples.es: I listened to music for a while.
We rested for a little while.
Please wait a little longer.
They'll be here in a moment.
Wrong: as a duration, 一会儿 goes after the verb: 我听了一会儿音乐。
Wrong: the duration goes before a noun object: 听了一会儿音乐。

notes: Also pronounced yìhuǐr in some dictionaries; the textbook form is yíhuìr.
The Grammar Wiki has no dedicated article on 一会儿; it's covered as a duration expression in the articles listed.

title: 又……又…… · Both … and …
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing "both A and B" with "you"” — not from the textbook
explanation: Put 又 (yòu) before each of two adjectives to say something has both qualities at once: 又快又舒服 (both fast and comfortable).
The two qualities should point the same way — both good (又便宜又好吃) or both bad (又贵又难吃). For a good point plus a bad point, use 可是 / 但是 instead.
The adjectives come straight after 又, without 很. The pattern also works with two verb phrases for doing two things at the same time: 他们又唱又跳.

patterns.label: Two qualities
patterns.formula: Subject + 又 + Adjective 1 + 又 + Adjective 2
examples: 现在坐高铁又快又舒服。

patterns.label: Two actions
patterns.formula: Subject + 又 + Verb 1 + 又 + Verb 2

examples.zh: 现在坐高铁又快又舒服。
examples.pinyin: Xiànzài zuò gāotiě yòu kuài yòu shūfu.
examples.es: Taking the high-speed train is now both fast and comfortable.

examples.pinyin: Zhège fángzi yòu dà yòu liàng.
examples.es: This house is both big and bright.

examples.pinyin: Zhōngguó cài yòu piányi yòu hǎochī.
examples.es: Chinese food is both cheap and tasty.

examples.zh: 这儿的咖啡又贵又不好喝。
examples.pinyin: Zhèr de kāfēi yòu guì yòu bù hǎohē.
examples.es: The coffee here is both expensive and not good.
Wrong: one quality is good and one bad; say 这件衣服很漂亮，可是太贵了。

notes: 又 on its own also means “again” for something that already happened (他又来了) — a different use.

title: 了…了 · Ongoing duration (“have been … for”)
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Expressing ongoing duration with double "le"” — not from the textbook
explanation: To say how long something lasted, the duration goes after the verb + 了: 我学了两年汉语 (“I studied Chinese for two years”). On its own this just reports a past period — you may have stopped since.
Add a second 了 at the very end of the sentence and the meaning changes to “up until now”: 我学了两年汉语了 means you have been studying for two years and still are. Think of the final 了 as “… and counting”.
If the verb has an object, either put the duration between the verb and the object (学了两年汉语了), or repeat the verb: 学汉语学了两年了.
To say how long you have NOT done something, the order changes: the duration comes first, then 没 + verb, and 了 goes at the end — 我三天没睡好了 (“I haven't slept well for three days”).

patterns.label: Ongoing duration
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + 了 + Duration (+ Object) + 了
examples: 我在这儿等了半个小时了。

patterns.label: Repeating the verb with an object
patterns.formula: Subject + Verb + Object + Verb + 了 + Duration + 了
examples: 她打电话打了一个小时了。

patterns.label: Duration of not doing something
patterns.formula: Subject + (已经) + Duration + 没 + Verb + 了

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Hànyǔ le.
examples.es: I've been studying Chinese for two years (and still am).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Hànyǔ.
examples.es: I studied Chinese for two years (it may be over now).

examples.zh: 我在这儿等了半个小时了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài zhèr děng le bàn ge xiǎoshí le.
examples.es: I've been waiting here for half an hour.

examples.pinyin: Tā xué Hànyǔ xué le yì nián le.
examples.es: He has been studying Chinese for a year.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ sān tiān méi shuìhǎo le.
examples.es: I haven't slept well for three days.
Wrong: with 没, the duration goes before 没 + verb.
Wrong: 了 goes right after the verb (学了两年汉语了 or 学汉语学了两年了).

notes: Without the final 了 the sentence doesn't say whether the action is still going on; with it, it clearly is.
已经 is often added for emphasis: 我已经等了一个小时了。 (Wǒ yǐjīng děngle yí ge xiǎoshí le. — I've already been waiting for an hour.)
To ask “how long have you…?”: 你学了多长时间汉语了？ (Nǐ xuéle duō cháng shíjiān Hànyǔ le?)
