title: 比 · Comparisons (“more … than”)
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Basic comparisons with "bi"” — not from the textbook
explanation: 比 works a bit like “than”, but it sits between the two things you compare, and the adjective comes last: A 比 B + adjective = “A is more [adj] than B”. Whatever comes first is the one that “wins”: 今天比昨天暖和 = today is warmer.
In a 比 sentence the adjective stands alone — no 很, 非常 or 真 before it. If you want to intensify, use 更 or 还 (“even more”) before the adjective. 还 sounds more surprised.
Any information about HOW MUCH more goes after the adjective: 多了 / 得多 (“much more”), 一点儿 (“a little more”), or an exact amount such as 两公分 or 三岁.
不比 is not the normal negative of 比. A 不比 B + adj means “A is no more … than B” — they're about the same — and is used to contradict what someone has said. For “not as … as”, use 没有.

patterns.label: Even more
patterns.formula: A + 比 + B + 更 / 还 + Adj

patterns.label: How much more
patterns.formula: A + 比 + B + Adj + 多了 / 得多 / 一点儿 / amount

examples.es: Today is warmer than yesterday.
Wrong: no 很 in a 比 sentence — say 暖和, 更暖和 or 暖和多了.

examples.pinyin: Zū de bǐ mǎi de piányi duō le.
examples.es: Renting is much cheaper than buying.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn bǐ nà jiàn cháng liǎng gōngfēn.
examples.es: This one is two centimeters longer than that one.
Wrong: the amount goes after the adjective.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de Hànyǔ bǐ wǒ hǎo.
examples.es: Your Chinese is better than mine.

examples.pinyin: Hóng de bù bǐ lǜ de piàoliang.
examples.es: The red one is no prettier than the green one (they're about the same).
Wrong: don't negate the adjective; say 我没有他高.

notes: 多了 can also be used without 比 when the comparison is clear from context: 最近天气暖和多了。 (Zuìjìn tiānqì nuǎnhuo duō le. — It's got much warmer lately.)
Don't mix 比 and 一样: for “as … as” use 跟 … 一样 (我跟他一样高).

title: 的字结构 · “The … one” (的 without a noun)
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Modifying nouns with adjective + "de"” — not from the textbook
explanation: Normally 的 links a description to a noun: 长的衣服 (“long clothes”), 我买的书 (“the book I bought”). When everyone already knows which noun you mean, you can drop it and keep just the description + 的.

The result works like a noun meaning “the one(s) that …”: 长的 = “the long one”, 新的 = “the new ones”, 我的 = “mine”, 租的 = “the rented one / renting”. It's the Chinese equivalent of English “one” in “the red one”.
This is very common when shopping or choosing: 我想要一件长的, 你要白的还是黑的？ It also lets you compare without repeating the noun: 新的比旧的贵.

patterns.label: Verb (phrase) + 的
patterns.formula: Verb + 的  (= the one that is Verb-ed)

examples.zh: 她的那件是短的，我想要一件长的。
examples.pinyin: Tā de nà jiàn shì duǎn de, wǒ xiǎng yào yí jiàn cháng de.
examples.es: Hers is a short one; I want a long one.

examples.pinyin: Xīn de bǐ jiù de guì.
examples.es: The new ones are more expensive than the old ones.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yào nǎ jiàn? —— Hóng de.
examples.es: Which one do you want? — The red one.

examples.pinyin: Zū de bǐ mǎi de piányi.
examples.es: Renting is cheaper than buying.
Wrong: without the noun you need 的 — 一件长的.

notes: A measure word can stay in front: 一件长的 (“a long one”), 那件红的 (“that red one”).
Only drop the noun when it's clear from context what you're talking about.

point: Adj + 一点儿 / 有点儿 + Adj (inferred)
title: 一点儿 / 有点儿 · “a bit more” vs. “a bit too”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Comparing "youdian" and "yidian"” — not from the textbook
explanation: Both mean “a little”, but they go in different places and do different jobs. 有点儿 goes BEFORE the adjective; 一点儿 goes AFTER it.
有点儿 + adjective describes something as “a bit too …” for your liking — it usually sounds like a mild complaint: 这件颜色有点儿深 (“this color is a bit (too) dark”).
Adjective + 一点儿 means “a bit more …” compared with something else. Use it to compare (这件比那件长一点儿), to ask for something different (有没有短一点儿的？) or to make a request (请说慢一点儿).
So a typical shopping exchange uses both: first the complaint with 有点儿, then the request with 一点儿 — 这件有点儿深，有没有浅一点儿的？

patterns.label: 一点儿 + noun (a little of something)

examples.es: The color of this one is a bit dark.
Do you have one that's a bit shorter?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng yào qiǎn yìdiǎnr de.
examples.es: I'd like one that's a bit lighter.
Wrong: to mean “a bit lighter”, 一点儿 goes after the adjective.
Wrong: before an adjective use 有点儿 — 今天有点儿冷.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn bǐ nà jiàn cháng yìdiǎnr.
examples.es: This one is a bit longer than that one.

notes: In casual speech both are often shortened: 有点 / 一点, or even just 点 after the adjective (便宜点吧！).
一点儿也不 + adjective means “not at all”: 这个菜一点儿也不辣。 (Zhège cài yìdiǎnr yě bú là. — This dish isn't spicy at all.)
有点儿 can go before 不 + a positive word: 她有点儿不舒服。 (Tā yǒudiǎnr bù shūfu. — She's not feeling very well.)

title: 或者 / 还是 · Two ways to say “or”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Comparing "haishi" and "huozhe"” — not from the textbook
explanation: English has one “or”; Chinese has two, and the choice depends on whether you're asking or stating.
还是 (háishi) is the “or” of questions: you offer options and expect the listener to pick one — 你要白的还是黑的？ The sentence is already a question, so it doesn't take 吗.
或者 (huòzhě) is the “or” of statements: it lists possibilities in a more relaxed way (“A, or maybe B, either is fine”) — 你们可以跳舞或者表演太极拳.
One catch: after phrases like 我不知道 or 我想知道, there is a hidden question inside the sentence, so you still use 还是: 我不知道他是老师还是学生.

patterns.label: 还是 in questions
patterns.formula: Option A + 还是 + Option B ？

patterns.label: 或者 in statements
patterns.formula: Option A + 或者 + Option B
examples: 你们可以跳舞或者表演太极拳。

patterns.label: 还是 in an embedded question
patterns.formula: 我不知道 / 我想知道 + A + 还是 + B
examples: 我不知道他是老师还是学生。

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yào bái de háishi hēi de?
examples.es: Do you want the white one or the black one?

examples.zh: 你们可以跳舞或者表演太极拳。
examples.pinyin: Nǐmen kěyǐ tiàowǔ huòzhě biǎoyǎn tàijíquán.
examples.es: You can dance or do a tai chi demonstration.
Wrong: in a question asking someone to choose, use 还是.
Either tomorrow or the day after is fine.
Wrong: this is a statement, so use 或者.

examples.zh: 我不知道他是老师还是学生。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào tā shì lǎoshī háishi xuésheng.
examples.es: I don't know whether he's a teacher or a student.

notes: Don't add 吗 to a 还是 question: ✗ 你喝茶还是喝咖啡吗？
还是 also has other meanings (“still”, “had better”), but as “or” it's for questions.

title: 没有 (那么) · “not as … as”
source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), “Basic comparisons with "meiyou"” — not from the textbook
explanation: 没有 can also be used to compare. A 没有 B + adjective means “A is not as [adj] as B” — the word order is the same as with 比, but the result is the opposite: here B is the one with more of the quality.
This is the usual way to negate a 比 sentence. 今天比昨天冷 (“today is colder”) becomes 今天没有昨天冷 (“today isn't as cold as yesterday”). Don't just put 不 in front of the adjective.
You can add 那么 (or 这么) before the adjective: 今天没有昨天那么冷. It means “as … as that”, and suggests that B really is quite [adj].
Compared with 不比, 没有 is the clear, everyday choice: 你没有我高 says you are definitely shorter, while 你不比我高 only says you're not taller (you might be the same height).

patterns.label: With 那么 / 这么
patterns.formula: A + 没有 + B + 那么 / 这么 + Adj
examples: 我的汉语没有你那么好。

patterns.label: Question form with 有
patterns.formula: A + 有 + B + (那么) + Adj + 吗？

examples.es: Today isn't as cold as yesterday.
Wrong: to negate a 比 comparison, use 没有 — 今天没有昨天冷.
Trains aren't as fast as planes.
Wrong: 多了, 一点儿 or an amount can't follow a 没有 comparison.

examples.zh: 我的汉语没有你那么好。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ de Hànyǔ méiyǒu nǐ nàme hǎo.
examples.es: My Chinese isn't as good as yours.
You're not as tall as me (I'm taller).

notes: Like with 比, don't put 很 or 非常 before the adjective: ✗ 今天没有昨天很冷.
没 alone is also common in speech: 今天没昨天冷。
